Only trivial differences…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only accessible primary description treats Kwasio (Mvumbo dialect) as a tone language with four contrastive lexical tones (H, L, HL, LH) and says nothing about word stress or accent. The only accent-related statement found is instrumental and cross-linguistic: Idiatov & Van de Velde's 2016 questionnaire recordings (Kwasio included) show lengthening of the stem-initial consonant, i.e. stem-initial prominence of the NW-Bantu type, which the authors derive from an utterance-level 'C-emphasis' (focus) prosody rather than lexical stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any source seen.
new_statements.exceptions: None in Ngue Um. Idiatov & Van de Velde note that the degree of stem-initial C-lengthening is greater under new-information or contrastive focus and can occasionally fall on prefixes under corrective focus (shown for Eton, not Kwasio).
new_statements.domain_note: Ngue Um: lexical tone on the word (citation forms and verb morphology). Idiatov & Van de Velde: stem-initial consonant duration measured in elicited questionnaire utterances; they argue the phenomenon is utterance-level emphasis phonologized onto the stem-initial position; no Kwasio-specific figures are shown in the slides.
new_statements.identity_note: Ngue Um 2002 describes the Mvùmbɔ̀ (Ngumba) dialect of Kwasio spoken around Lolodorf/Kribi, Cameroon (informants from Nkumbala); Kwasio [nmg, kwas1243] also comprises the Mabi (Kribi coast) and Bisio/Bujeba (Equatorial Guinea) varieties, not covered. Idiatov & Van de Velde recorded 'Kwasio' (dialect unstated) and separately Bagyeli (= Gyeli, gyel1242, a distinct Glottolog language already in the catalog).

Besides the level tones H and L, he also finds two contour tones: LH and HL. [p. 522:] The stem-initial position generally appears as the strongest. [...] In general, the other positions are prosodically weaker and liable to show restrictions (segmental ones in particular).

new_statements.relation_note: Same picture as the existing Ngue Um 2002 statement (tone language, no stress statement); the p. 522 remark on stem-initial positional strength is a compatible, group-level (A80) refinement about positional prominence, not a stress placement claim.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kwasio (mvumbo variety) is described as a tone language with H and B (L) level tones (M rare) plus BH and HB contours; the Kwasio phonology sketch contains no statement on word stress or accent (the words accent/accentué/proéminence/tonique do not occur in the section, and 'accent' does not occur anywhere in the thesis). The only prominence remark is a general, positional one for the A80 group: the stem-initial position is prosodically the strongest, the other positions weaker and subject to segmental restrictions and erosion.
new_statements.exceptions: none; note the sources disagree on tone registers (Woungly-Massaga 1971: H, M, B; Bouh Ma Sitna 2006 and Ngue Um 2006: H, B with M rare/grammatical)
new_statements.identity_note: Cheucle 2014 (p. 194, fn. 176) states that her Kwasio sketch and comparative data concern the mvumbo variety, 'aussi ngumba, renvoyant à une seule et même variété' (mvumbo = ngumba), the variety of kwas1243; her lexical data are from Duke 2004 (mvumbo, without tones). Skolaster 1910 would describe Ngumba as spoken c. 1910 around Kribi/Lolodorf but could not be opened.

new_statements.quote: Betonung. Der Ton liegt in der Regel auf der vorletzten Silbe. Einsilbige Wörter behalten auch in der Mehrheit den Ton auf dem Stamm, wenn der Stammvokal lang ist; ist der Stammvokal dagegen kurz, so tritt der Ton auf das Präfix zurück, z. B. bê Schmerz, mabê, dagegen fu Fisch bófu. Mehrsilbige Wörter, die auf ñ endigen, haben den Ton auf der letzten Silbe, z. B. piuñ Wunde, luañ bauen. Im Imperativ der Verba rückt der Ton gern auf das Suffix, z. B. luangá, luangánga. Auch das Endungs-o des [p. 80] Inf. Pass. wird gewöhnlich betont. In zweifelhaften Fällen gibt das Zeichen ' an, daß der Ton auf der bezeichneten Silbe liegt.
new_statements.translation: Accentuation. The accent lies as a rule on the penultimate syllable. Monosyllabic words keep the accent on the stem in the plural too, if the stem vowel is long; if the stem vowel is short, the accent moves back onto the prefix, e.g. bê 'pain', mabê, but fu 'fish', bófu. Polysyllabic words ending in ñ have the accent on the last syllable, e.g. piuñ 'wound', luañ 'build'. In the imperative of verbs the accent readily moves onto the suffix, e.g. luangá, luangánga. The final -o of the passive infinitive is also usually accented. In doubtful cases the sign ' indicates that the accent lies on the marked syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Type and placement differ from what is on record. The catalog codes Mvumbo/Kwasio as tonal (four lexical tones, Ngue Um 2002; H/B + contours, Cheucle 2014) with no stress rule, and the A80 literature held by the project (Cheucle 2014 p. 522; Idiatov & Van de Velde 2016) places prominence stem-INITIALLY. Skolaster 1910, a pre-tonological missionary grammar, describes no lexical tone and instead states a PENULTIMATE word accent with morphologically and length-conditioned exceptions (prefix accent in bófu, final accent on -ñ words, suffix accent in imperatives/passives). For prefixless disyllabic stems penult and stem-initial coincide, but his prefix-accented plurals (bófu) and suffix-accented…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Skolaster gives a 'Betonung' rule: the accent ('Ton') lies as a rule on the penultimate syllable. Stated exceptions: monosyllabic (stem) nouns keep the accent on the stem in the plural if the stem vowel is long, but if it is short the accent retracts onto the plural prefix (fu 'fish' -> bófu); polysyllabic words ending in ñ (velar nasal) are accented on the final syllable (piuñ, luañ); in the imperative the accent tends to move onto the suffix (luangá, luangánga); the passive-infinitive ending -o is usually accented (jambo 'cook' vs jambó 'be cooked', p. 93: passive 'durch die Verschiebung des Akzentes kenntlich'); in the auxiliaries 'be' the accent rests on the personal prefix in present, imperfect and perfect (p. 80). An acute mark is written on the accented syllable in doubtful cases. Lexical tone is not described anywhere in the grammar (questions are said to be marked 'durch Hebung der Stimme', p. 81); Nekes's introduction mentions musical tone only for Jaunde (p. 73).
new_statements.exceptions: plural of short-vowel monosyllabic stems: accent on prefix (bófu); words ending in ñ: final accent (piuñ, luañ); imperatives: accent on suffix (luangá, luangánga); passive infinitive -o usually accented (jambó); auxiliaries: accent on the personal prefix in present/imperfect/perfect
new_statements.identity_note: Skolaster describes Ngumba (= Mvumbo; 'Die Ngumba, oder besser Mvumbo, von den Jaunde Mekuk genannt'), the Kwasio variety spoken around Lolodorf-Bipindi on the Kribi-Jaunde road (Catholic Pallottine mission), with bracketed notes on Mabea (Mabi) pronunciation differences; this is the Mvumbo/Ngumba dialect the catalog record names. Schadeberg 1980 is a comparative paper on Common Bantu and Cameroonian Bantu verb morphology, not a Kwasio description.

readall_conflicts: Skolaster 1910 (now obtained and read) states a word accent that falls 'in der Regel auf der vorletzten Silbe' (penultimate), with prefix accent in plurals of short-vowel monosyllabic stems (bófu), final accent on words in -ñ, and suffix accent in imperatives and passive infinitives (jambo vs jambó), and never describes lexical tone. This disagrees with the record in two ways: the catalog and both verified statements held by the project (Ngue Um 2002: four lexical tones; Cheucle 2014: H/B plus contour tones) treat Mvumbo/Kwasio as tonal with no stress rule, and the A80 prosody literature held by the project (Cheucle 2014 p. 522, Idiatov & Van de Velde 2016) locates prominence stem-initially rather than on the penult. The 1910 statement is a pre-tonemic missionary description whose 'Ton/Akzent' very likely records tone and length percepts as stress; it should be staged as a historical stress statement alongside the tonal coding, not override it. Schadeberg 1980 remains unread (Leiden OA copy captcha-could not be reached by automated download); it is a 7-page Common Bantu morphology paper and is not expected to bear on Kwasio prosody.

sources.note: Instrumental questionnaire study; Kwasio (2 men, ca. 35 min) and Bagyeli among nine recorded NW Bantu languages (slide 7). Slide 10: 'Stem-initial consonant length in all languages (set #1), except Bapuku (and Orungu, set #2), which have penultimate vowel length'. Authors interpret stem-initial C-lengthening as stem-initial accent originating in utterance-level 'C-emphasis prosody' (focus). sources.note: Secondhand via Cheucle 2014:214: 'Ngue Um (2006: 18-19) adopte une approche autosegmentale et met en exergue les schemes tonals permettant de rendre compte a la fois des tons ponctuels et des tons modules. En surface, il releve trois niveaux de hauteur melodique: H, B, M. Le ton M est assez rare en kwasio.. Il semble surtout present sous forme de ton grammatical mais il apparait aussi comme ton lexical' and (p.19) a structural analysis treating the contour tones as tonemes.
sources.venue: Mémoire de DEA, Université de Yaoundé I

sources.note: Secondhand via Cheucle 2014:214: 'Bouh Ma Sitna (2006: 14), quant a lui, releve deux registres, H et B. En plus des tons ponctuels H et B, il releve egalement deux tons modules: BH et HB.' i.e. two level tones (H, L) plus rising LH and falling HL contours; also six syllable types (p.176 of extract) and vowel/consonant charts pp.4-13.
